Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.'}, {'author': 'Daniel', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a flexible and effective approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment. Across vision, language, and structured prediction tasks, distillation methods that go beyond matching output logits—by leveraging intermediate representations, adaptive teacher-student interaction, adversarial examples, and task-aware selection—consistently improve student performance while addressing practical constraints such as inference speed, memory, and robustness. Combining distillation with complementary techniques (progressive replacing, pruning, or route-constrained supervision) further mitigates capacity gaps and teacher limitations, making distillation a practical centerpiece of model-compression toolkits.'}, {'author': 'Rogers', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing', 'abstract': 'In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.'}, {'author': 'Fowler', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression', 'abstract': "Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation."}, {'author': 'Reid', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, efficient models by transferring information from one or more teacher models to a student model. The literature shows a wide variety of objectives and mechanisms for KD — from soft-target matching and internal representation alignment to adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-inspired routes — and covers applications across vision, ranking, summarization, machine translation, and reinforcement learning. Trade-offs reported across studies include teacher–student capacity gap effects, data requirements, computational cost, robustness and generalization properties, and task-specific adaptations. Practical recipes include multi-teacher weighting, layer-wise and task-aware filters, progressive module replacement, and combinations of pruning with distillation.'}, {'author': 'Robinson', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Adversarially Robust Distillation', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.'}, {'author': 'Walker', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Pre-trained Summarization Distillation', 'abstract': "Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz."}, {'author': 'Jackson', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students). Approaches span soft-target (logit) matching, transferring intermediate/internal representations, layer-wise and module-level mimicry, adversarial and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision and NLP shows KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance, but success depends on factors such as teacher-student capacity gap, the form of distilled knowledge, task alignment, and the data used for distillation. Contemporary research emphasizes task-aware selection of distilled signals, improving teacher-student compatibility, and preserving robustness and decision-boundary information to make distillation more effective in practice.'}, {'author': 'Montgomery', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'The Case for Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into efficient students for deployment. However, its success is not uniform: different distillation strategies transfer different kinds of knowledge, interact with model capacity and data complexity, and trade off accuracy, robustness, and cost. I argue that the most reliable path to compact, high-quality models—especially in NLP—is to adopt task-aware, representation-focused distillation that (1) aligns intermediate representations selectively to the target task, (2) uses adaptive teacher schedules or multi-teacher weighting to reduce capability gaps, and (3) integrates distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacing). This combined stance balances effectiveness, computational cost, and robustness, and is supported by empirical and theoretical analyses across vision, language, retrieval, and sequence generation settings.'}, {'author': 'Herrera', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP: Effective Practices and Limitations', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, more deployable students. KD improves inference efficiency while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, but its success depends on choices of what knowledge is transferred, how the teacher and student are coupled, the match between student capacity and task complexity, and whether distillation is combined with other compression methods. Practitioners should select distillation strategies that target internal representations, task-relevant signals, and robustness properties, and consider alternative or complementary methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when data, latency, or robustness constraints dictate different trade-offs."}, {'author': 'Bowman', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods for Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related compression methods form a diverse toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Approaches include classic soft-label distillation, intermediate-representation (layer/hint) matching, contrastive and distributional alignment, adversarial and robustness-focused strategies, teacher-design and selection methods, and structural compression (e.g., pruning and progressive module replacement). Empirical work across vision, NLP, ranking, translation, summarization, reinforcement learning, and 3D/pose tasks demonstrates practical trade-offs between accuracy, robustness, data requirements, and inference latency.'}, {'author': 'Shaffer', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation', 'abstract': 'The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.'}, {'author': 'Abbott', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs', 'abstract': '3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.'}, {'author': 'Gardner', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation', 'abstract': 'Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.'}, {'author': 'Miller', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy large deep models by transferring aspects of teacher models into smaller students, or by surgically removing capacity via pruning. Research across vision, NLP, ranking, reinforcement learning and 3D detection has developed many complementary distillation formulations (soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, layer-wise alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and pruning-aware strategies) as well as strategies for choosing or evolving teachers. Results show that distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while improving latency and storage, can improve robustness or continual-learning behavior when adapted appropriately, and interacts nontrivially with dataset complexity and student capacity. Practical trade-offs remain: some distillation variants require extra unlabeled data or expensive teacher ensembles, while pruning-based methods can achieve high sparsity and speedups without distillation at the cost of different engineering considerations.'}, {'author': 'Calderon', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Mechanisms, and Best Practices', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones in both vision and NLP. Practical success depends on aligning the distilled signals with the student capacity and the target task: task-aware selection of teacher information, attention to internal representations, dynamic or meta-learned teacher strategies, and robustness-aware objectives all improve outcomes. Depending on constraints (data availability, latency, robustness), alternatives like structured pruning or parameter shrinking may be preferable or used in concert with KD.'}, {'author': 'Zuniga', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of approaches for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance of large teacher models. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, or decision-boundary information), how teachers and students are paired or trained (fixed teachers, learned student-friendly teachers, evolutionary or online teachers, multi-teacher ensembles), and whether complementary compression such as pruning is used. Empirical work across vision, NLP, ranking, summarization and reinforcement learning shows that targeted choices about the distillation signal, teacher selection, and task-awareness substantially affect student quality, robustness, and inference efficiency. Remaining challenges include closing capability gaps between teachers and students, reducing dependence on large unlabeled datasets, and ensuring transfer of internal and robustness properties.'}, {'author': 'Roman', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Improving Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation for Natural Language Understanding', 'abstract': 'This paper explores the use of knowledge distillation to improve a Multi-Task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) (Liu et al., 2019) for learning text representations across multiple natural language understanding tasks. Although ensemble learning can improve model performance, serving an ensemble of large DNNs such as MT-DNN can be prohibitively expensive. Here we apply the knowledge distillation method (Hinton et al., 2015) in the multi-task learning setting. For each task, we train an ensemble of different MT-DNNs (teacher) that outperforms any single model, and then train a single MT-DNN (student) via multi-task learning to \\emph{distill} knowledge from these ensemble teachers. We show that the distilled MT-DNN significantly outperforms the original MT-DNN on 7 out of 9 GLUE tasks, pushing the GLUE benchmark (single model) to 83.7\\% (1.5\\% absolute improvement\\footnote{ Based on the GLUE leaderboard at https://gluebenchmark.com/leaderboard as of April 1, 2019.}). The code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available at https://github.com/namisan/mt-dnn.'}, {'author': 'Roberts', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer the predictive power of large models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Empirical results show KD can recover much of teacher performance in many settings, but success depends on teacher-student capacity gaps, the form of transferred knowledge, availability of data, and task properties. The literature has proposed principled analyses and practical recipes for improving transfer, consolidating state-of-the-art compression workflows for NLP tasks such as classification, translation, ranking, and summarization.'}, {'author': 'Munoz', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Structured Pruning Learns Compact and Accurate Models', 'abstract': 'The growing size of neural language models has led to increased attention in model compression. The two predominant approaches are pruning, which gradually removes weights from a pre-trained model, and distillation, which trains a smaller compact model to match a larger one. Pruning methods can significantly reduce the model size but hardly achieve large speedups as distillation. However, distillation methods require large amounts of unlabeled data and are expensive to train. In this work, we propose a task-specific structured pruning method CoFi (Coarse- and Fine-grained Pruning), which delivers highly parallelizable subnetworks and matches the distillation methods in both accuracy and latency, without resorting to any unlabeled data. Our key insight is to jointly prune coarse-grained (e.g., layers) and fine-grained (e.g., heads and hidden units) modules, which controls the pruning decision of each parameter with masks of different granularity. We also devise a layerwise distillation strategy to transfer knowledge from unpruned to pruned models during optimization. Our experiments on GLUE and SQuAD datasets show that CoFi yields models with over 10x speedups with a small accuracy drop, showing its effectiveness and efficiency compared to previous pruning and distillation approaches.'}, {'author': 'Hill', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning', 'abstract': 'We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.'}, {'author': 'Ramirez', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP (2017–2022)', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Across vision, speech, reinforcement learning and NLP, the field has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, feature-map and inter-channel correlation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, module-replacement and progressive shrinking, and hybrid approaches that combine distillation with structured pruning. Empirical work shows these techniques can preserve accuracy while delivering large parameter and latency reductions, but success depends on choices such as what to transfer (logits vs. intermediate features), how to schedule or construct the teacher (fixed, learned, or progressive), the student capacity and task complexity, and available unlabeled data. Recent efforts also address robustness, decision-boundary alignment, and task-aware filtering, and alternative compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning) can match distillation in some settings when combined with task-specific transfer. Remaining challenges include capacity gaps between teachers and students, the need for large or carefully distilled data in sequence-generation tasks, and ensuring reliable transfer of internal structure rather than only matching outputs.'}, {'author': 'Bush', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones. When applied thoughtfully—by transferring not only logits but also internal representations, by tailoring teacher selection and training, and by addressing adversarial robustness—distillation can match or approach the performance of large models while delivering major gains in latency and footprint. However, the best distillation recipe depends strongly on the task, the capacity gap between teacher and student, and constraints such as data availability and robustness requirements.'}, {'author': 'Williams', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to deploy large deep models by training smaller students to capture the behavior of larger teachers or ensembles. Work across computer vision, NLP, and reinforcement learning has developed complementary approaches: soft-target distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, multi- and online-teacher strategies, confidence- and task-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and techniques that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. These methods trade off fidelity to the teacher, training cost, data requirements, robustness, and runtime efficiency; their empirical success depends on design choices such as what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations), how teachers are selected or learned, and whether the process is offline, online, or self-distillation. The literature shows that (1) distillation often reduces the effective complexity of training data and eases learning for constrained student architectures, (2) internal-representation losses, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, and route or curriculum strategies can substantially improve transfer, and (3) distillation can be combined with pruning or adversarial objectives to yield compact, fast, and sometimes robust models. Practical application requires matching the distillation recipe to task characteristics, data availability, and the student capacity.'}, {'author': 'Martin', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Distillation as the Practical Core of NLP Model Compression: Representation-, Task-, and Robustness-aware Strategies', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and practical approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. When distillation goes beyond matching soft labels and targets internal representations, task-relevant components, and teacher-student dynamics (including teacher selection and robustness), it consistently yields better compressed models for NLP tasks. However, distillation is not a one-size-fits-all solution: different compression objectives (latency, data constraints, robustness) call for different distillation recipes or hybridization with pruning and parameter-replacement methods. I argue that representation- and task-aware distillation, combined with careful teacher design/selection and robustness-aware procedures, provides the best overall tradeoff for compressing NLP models in practice.'}, {'author': 'Adams', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Effective Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis and Recommendations', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language tasks shows that no single distillation recipe is universally optimal; instead, combining complementary strategies — transferring internal representations, applying layer- and task-aware selection, adapting or learning teacher behaviors, and using contrastive/adversarial objectives — yields better student models and more robust compression. Practical trade-offs with pruning and task-specific choices (e.g., parallel NAT decoders or abstractive summarizers) must guide method selection. Below I synthesize evidence from recent studies and give concrete prescriptions for applying KD effectively in deep learning and NLP.'}, {'author': 'Hall', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Why Knowledge Distillation Remains Central to Efficient NLP Models — and How to Make It Better', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a practical and flexible approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Its success spans supervised tasks, multi-task systems, ensembles, and specialized settings like non-autoregressive translation, ranking, and summarization. However, distillation has known weaknesses (data requirements, capacity gaps, robustness) that motivate complementary or improved algorithms. Combining distillation with task-aware, representational, adversarial, or pruning-based techniques produces more compact and reliable models suitable for production NLP systems.'}, {'author': 'Santos', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.'}, {'author': 'Mcclain', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.'}]

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Distilling Dense Representations for Ranking using Tightly-Coupled Teachers
papers_seen.abstract: We present an approach to ranking with dense representations that applies knowledge distillation to improve the recently proposed late-interaction ColBERT model. Specifically, we distill the knowledge from ColBERT's expressive MaxSim operator for computing relevance scores into a simple dot product, thus enabling single-step ANN search. Our key insight is that during distillation, tight coupling between the teacher model and the student model enables more flexible distillation strategies and yields better learned representations. We empirically show that our approach improves query latency and greatly reduces the onerous storage requirements of ColBERT, while only making modest sacrifices in terms of effectiveness. By combining our dense representations with sparse representations derived from document expansion, we are able to approach the effectiveness of a standard cross-encoder reranker using BERT that is orders of magnitude slower.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches range from matching output probabilities to aligning intermediate representations, using single or multiple teachers, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and task-aware layer filtering. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, and reinforcement learning shows distillation can improve student accuracy, speed, and sometimes robustness, but its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity gap, the form of transferred knowledge, data availability, and task-specific constraints. Complementary compression methods such as structured pruning can match or exceed distillation on some latency metrics while avoiding unlabeled-data costs. Recent innovations focus on better aligning internal representations, dynamically selecting or evolving teachers, preserving robustness, and reducing the difficulty gap between teacher and student to improve transfer.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from teacher models to student models. Research has advanced along multiple axes: (1) what knowledge is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations, decision-boundary samples, etc.), (2) when and how the teacher and student are trained (offline pre-trained teachers, joint / online / evolutionary teachers, meta-learned teachers, progressive replacement), (3) specialized objectives and architectures for transfer (adversarial objectives, Wasserstein-based contrastive losses, layer-wise/task-aware filters, route-constrained curricula), and (4) applications and tradeoffs in domains such as image classification, non-autoregressive translation, summarization, ranking, detection, reinforcement learning, and continual learning. Empirical work shows that appropriate choice of knowledge, coupling between teacher and student, and task-aware filtering substantially affects final student accuracy, robustness, and latency. Ongoing challenges include closing the capacity gap for very small students, preserving robustness and internal representations, and reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora for distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP (2017–2022)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Across vision, speech, reinforcement learning and NLP, the field has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include internal-representation matching, feature-map and inter-channel correlation alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, module-replacement and progressive shrinking, and hybrid approaches that combine distillation with structured pruning. Empirical work shows these techniques can preserve accuracy while delivering large parameter and latency reductions, but success depends on choices such as what to transfer (logits vs. intermediate features), how to schedule or construct the teacher (fixed, learned, or progressive), the student capacity and task complexity, and available unlabeled data. Recent efforts also address robustness, decision-boundary alignment, and task-aware filtering, and alternative compression strategies (e.g., structured pruning) can match distillation in some settings when combined with task-specific transfer. Remaining challenges include capacity gaps between teachers and students, the need for large or carefully distilled data in sequence-generation tasks, and ensuring reliable transfer of internal structure rather than only matching outputs.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and its Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning based models are relatively large, and it is hard to deploy such models on resource-limited devices such as mobile phones and embedded devices. One possible solution is knowledge distillation whereby a smaller model (student model) is trained by utilizing the information from a larger model (teacher model). In this paper, we present a survey of knowledge distillation techniques applied to deep learning models. To compare the performances of different techniques, we propose a new metric called distillation metric. Distillation metric compares different knowledge distillation algorithms based on sizes and accuracy scores. Based on the survey, some interesting conclusions are drawn and presented in this paper.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones in both vision and NLP. KD works through multiple mechanisms — smoothing, class-relationship transfer, and instance-level guidance — and can be combined with complementary techniques such as structured pruning, module replacement, and curriculum-style training. Practical success depends on aligning the distilled signals with the student capacity and the target task: task-aware selection of teacher information, attention to internal representations, dynamic or meta-learned teacher strategies, and robustness-aware objectives all improve outcomes. Depending on constraints (data availability, latency, robustness), alternatives like structured pruning or parameter shrinking may be preferable or used in concert with KD.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become core tools for transferring knowledge from larger, expensive models to smaller, efficient models. Research has developed multiple complementary strategies — logit/soft-label distillation, internal/feature-level matching, layer-wise and module-wise transfer, multi-teacher and ensemble-based approaches, adversarial and curriculum-based methods, and combinations with pruning — and applied them across vision, language, ranking, and reinforcement learning tasks. Advances emphasize matching representations that matter for a target task, selecting trustworthy or tightly-coupled supervision signals, and shaping the distillation process (e.g., via progressive replacement, teacher evolution, or task-aware filtering) to close capability gaps between teacher and student while preserving performance, robustness, and runtime efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Task-Aware, Representation-Centric Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a mature and indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into compact, deployable students. Its success depends not only on reusing teacher logits but on matching internal structure, selecting task-relevant information, and adapting the distillation strategy to model capacity and data complexity. Combining representation-level alignment, dynamic multi-teacher strategies, and task-aware pruning or replacement yields the best trade-offs between size, speed, and accuracy in practical NLP and deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Student Network Learning via Evolutionary Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation provides an effective way to transfer knowledge via teacher-student learning, where most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model as teacher to supervise the learning of student network. This manner usually brings in a big capability gap between teacher and student networks during learning. Recent researches have observed that a small teacher-student capability gap can facilitate knowledge transfer. Inspired by that, we propose an evolutionary knowledge distillation approach to improve the transfer effectiveness of teacher knowledge. Instead of a fixed pre-trained teacher, an evolutionary teacher is learned online and consistently transfers intermediate knowledge to supervise student network learning on-the-fly. To enhance intermediate knowledge representation and mimicking, several simple guided modules are introduced between corresponding teacher-student blocks. In this way, the student can simultaneously obtain rich internal knowledge and capture its growth process, leading to effective student network learning. Extensive experiments clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach as well as good adaptability in the low-resolution and few-sample visual recognition scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to deploy large deep models by training smaller students to capture the behavior of larger teachers or ensembles. Work across computer vision, NLP, and reinforcement learning has developed complementary approaches: soft-target distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, multi- and online-teacher strategies, confidence- and task-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and techniques that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. These methods trade off fidelity to the teacher, training cost, data requirements, robustness, and runtime efficiency; their empirical success depends on design choices such as what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations), how teachers are selected or learned, and whether the process is offline, online, or self-distillation. The literature shows that (1) distillation often reduces the effective complexity of training data and eases learning for constrained student architectures, (2) internal-representation losses, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, and route or curriculum strategies can substantially improve transfer, and (3) distillation can be combined with pruning or adversarial objectives to yield compact, fast, and sometimes robust models. Practical application requires matching the distillation recipe to task characteristics, data availability, and the student capacity.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students). Over the past decade methods have moved beyond simple output-probability (soft-label) matching to leverage internal representations, layer-wise alignment, adversarial objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble sources, online or evolving teachers, and task-aware compression strategies. In NLP, KD is widely used to compress large pretrained transformers for downstream tasks, but choices about what to transfer and how to schedule or weight supervision have important trade-offs for accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. Key open challenges include closing the teacher–student capacity gap, reducing reliance on large unlabeled corpora for distillation, and preserving robustness and task-specific information while obtaining practical speedups.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Adaptive, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Effective Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful and versatile technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Its success depends not only on transferring final soft targets but also on aligning internal representations, selecting appropriate teacher signals, and adapting distillation strategies to task constraints and student capacity. A suite of complementary approaches — attention- and feature-based matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, and hybrid pruning–distillation workflows — improves transfer effectiveness and addresses challenges such as capacity gap, data requirements, and robustness. When chosen and combined appropriately, these methods make distillation practical for real-world NLP and vision systems, enabling large gains in latency, storage, and sometimes even robustness without wholesale accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones. When applied thoughtfully—by transferring not only logits but also internal representations, by tailoring teacher selection and training, and by addressing adversarial robustness—distillation can match or approach the performance of large models while delivering major gains in latency and footprint. However, the best distillation recipe depends strongly on the task, the capacity gap between teacher and student, and constraints such as data availability and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Principles, Trade-offs, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and reinforcement learning, KD variants improve student models by transferring teacher knowledge at outputs, intermediate representations, or via alternate training curricula. However, KD is not a panacea: choices about what to transfer (logits, internal features, attention maps), how to form teachers (fixed, evolving, ensemble, or self-teaching), and whether to combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning or structured sparsity) materially affect outcomes. I argue that (1) principled transfer of internal and task-relevant representations is essential for robust compression; (2) adaptive teacher selection, confidence-aware weighting, and adversarially-informed samples improve student generalization; and (3) pruning and module-replacement techniques are practical complements to KD when data or compute budgets constrain distillation. Based on survey and empirical results across tasks, I outline actionable best practices for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy large deep models by transferring aspects of teacher models into smaller students, or by surgically removing capacity via pruning. Research across vision, NLP, ranking, reinforcement learning and 3D detection has developed many complementary distillation formulations (soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, layer-wise alignment, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, and pruning-aware strategies) as well as strategies for choosing or evolving teachers. Results show that distillation can preserve much of teacher accuracy while improving latency and storage, can improve robustness or continual-learning behavior when adapted appropriately, and interacts nontrivially with dataset complexity and student capacity. Practical trade-offs remain: some distillation variants require extra unlabeled data or expensive teacher ensembles, while pruning-based methods can achieve high sparsity and speedups without distillation at the cost of different engineering considerations.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The primary goal of knowledge distillation (KD) is to encapsulate the information of a model learned from a teacher network into a student network, with the latter being more compact than the former. Existing work, e.g., using Kullback-Leibler divergence for distillation, may fail to capture important structural knowledge in the teacher network and often lacks the ability for feature generalization, particularly in situations when teacher and student are built to address different classification tasks. We propose Wasserstein Contrastive Representation Distillation (WCoRD), which leverages both primal and dual forms of Wasserstein distance for KD. The dual form is used for global knowledge transfer, yielding a contrastive learning objective that maximizes the lower bound of mutual information between the teacher and the student networks. The primal form is used for local contrastive knowledge transfer within a mini-batch, effectively matching the distributions of features between the teacher and the student networks. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed WCoRD method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on privileged information distillation, model compression and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. KD is most effective when its design is matched to the task and student capacity: techniques that go beyond simple soft-label matching—by leveraging internal representations, task-aware layer selection, multi-teacher signals, learned teachers or teacher trajectories, and complementary pruning or robustness objectives—consistently yield better compressed models for both vision and NLP. Rather than a single recipe, the literature indicates a family of distillation strategies that should be selected or combined according to model architecture, task complexity, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP: Effective Practices and Limitations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, more deployable students. KD improves inference efficiency while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, but its success depends on choices of what knowledge is transferred, how the teacher and student are coupled, the match between student capacity and task complexity, and whether distillation is combined with other compression methods. Practitioners should select distillation strategies that target internal representations, task-relevant signals, and robustness properties, and consider alternative or complementary methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when data, latency, or robustness constraints dictate different trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, efficient models by transferring information from one or more teacher models to a student model. The literature shows a wide variety of objectives and mechanisms for KD — from soft-target matching and internal representation alignment to adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-inspired routes — and covers applications across vision, ranking, summarization, machine translation, and reinforcement learning. Trade-offs reported across studies include teacher–student capacity gap effects, data requirements, computational cost, robustness and generalization properties, and task-specific adaptations. Practical recipes include multi-teacher weighting, layer-wise and task-aware filters, progressive module replacement, and combinations of pruning with distillation.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible and effective approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment. Across vision, language, and structured prediction tasks, distillation methods that go beyond matching output logits—by leveraging intermediate representations, adaptive teacher-student interaction, adversarial examples, and task-aware selection—consistently improve student performance while addressing practical constraints such as inference speed, memory, and robustness. Combining distillation with complementary techniques (progressive replacing, pruning, or route-constrained supervision) further mitigates capacity gaps and teacher limitations, making distillation a practical centerpiece of model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Structured Pruning Learns Compact and Accurate Models
papers_seen.abstract: The growing size of neural language models has led to increased attention in model compression. The two predominant approaches are pruning, which gradually removes weights from a pre-trained model, and distillation, which trains a smaller compact model to match a larger one. Pruning methods can significantly reduce the model size but hardly achieve large speedups as distillation. However, distillation methods require large amounts of unlabeled data and are expensive to train. In this work, we propose a task-specific structured pruning method CoFi (Coarse- and Fine-grained Pruning), which delivers highly parallelizable subnetworks and matches the distillation methods in both accuracy and latency, without resorting to any unlabeled data. Our key insight is to jointly prune coarse-grained (e.g., layers) and fine-grained (e.g., heads and hidden units) modules, which controls the pruning decision of each parameter with masks of different granularity. We also devise a layerwise distillation strategy to transfer knowledge from unpruned to pruned models during optimization. Our experiments on GLUE and SQuAD datasets show that CoFi yields models with over 10x speedups with a small accuracy drop, showing its effectiveness and efficiency compared to previous pruning and distillation approaches.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer the predictive power of large models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Research across vision, reinforcement learning, and NLP has produced a wide set of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate representation matching, layer-wise or module replacement, adversarial and contrastive objectives, curriculum-based routes, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structured pruning—that trade off fidelity, compute cost, and data requirements. Empirical results show KD can recover much of teacher performance in many settings, but success depends on teacher-student capacity gaps, the form of transferred knowledge, availability of data, and task properties. The literature has proposed principled analyses and practical recipes for improving transfer, consolidating state-of-the-art compression workflows for NLP tasks such as classification, translation, ranking, and summarization.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: The Case for Task-Aware, Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into efficient students for deployment. However, its success is not uniform: different distillation strategies transfer different kinds of knowledge, interact with model capacity and data complexity, and trade off accuracy, robustness, and cost. I argue that the most reliable path to compact, high-quality models—especially in NLP—is to adopt task-aware, representation-focused distillation that (1) aligns intermediate representations selectively to the target task, (2) uses adaptive teacher schedules or multi-teacher weighting to reduce capability gaps, and (3) integrates distillation with complementary compression techniques (e.g., structured pruning or progressive replacing). This combined stance balances effectiveness, computational cost, and robustness, and is supported by empirical and theoretical analyses across vision, language, retrieval, and sequence generation settings.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Effective Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language tasks shows that no single distillation recipe is universally optimal; instead, combining complementary strategies — transferring internal representations, applying layer- and task-aware selection, adapting or learning teacher behaviors, and using contrastive/adversarial objectives — yields better student models and more robust compression. Practical trade-offs with pruning and task-specific choices (e.g., parallel NAT decoders or abstractive summarizers) must guide method selection. Below I synthesize evidence from recent studies and give concrete prescriptions for applying KD effectively in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. A wide range of KD strategies—matching soft targets, aligning internal representations, adversarial transfers, multi-teacher schemes, and progressive module replacement—have proven effective across vision, ranking, and NLP tasks. Best results arise when distillation methods are chosen or combined to match the task and constraints: internal- and layer-wise alignment help transfer structural features, teacher training and trajectory-aware approaches improve transferability, adversarial and contrastive formulations capture richer knowledge, and alternatives such as structured pruning or simplified shrink-and-fine-tune procedures can be preferable under specific data or latency constraints. Practical adoption therefore benefits from a taxonomy of KD techniques and task-aware selection of methods.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Adaptive, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Effective Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful and versatile technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Its success depends not only on transferring final soft targets but also on aligning internal representations, selecting appropriate teacher signals, and adapting distillation strategies to task constraints and student capacity. A suite of complementary approaches — attention- and feature-based matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer selection, and hybrid pruning–distillation workflows — improves transfer effectiveness and addresses challenges such as capacity gap, data requirements, and robustness. When chosen and combined appropriately, these methods make distillation practical for real-world NLP and vision systems, enabling large gains in latency, storage, and sometimes even robustness without wholesale accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Principles, Trade-offs, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, ranking, summarization, translation, and reinforcement learning, KD variants improve student models by transferring teacher knowledge at outputs, intermediate representations, or via alternate training curricula. However, KD is not a panacea: choices about what to transfer (logits, internal features, attention maps), how to form teachers (fixed, evolving, ensemble, or self-teaching), and whether to combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning or structured sparsity) materially affect outcomes. I argue that (1) principled transfer of internal and task-relevant representations is essential for robust compression; (2) adaptive teacher selection, confidence-aware weighting, and adversarially-informed samples improve student generalization; and (3) pruning and module-replacement techniques are practical complements to KD when data or compute budgets constrain distillation. Based on survey and empirical results across tasks, I outline actionable best practices for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Pre-trained Summarization Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent state-of-the-art approaches to summarization utilize large pre-trained Transformer models. Distilling these models to smaller student models has become critically important for practical use; however there are many different distillation methods proposed by the NLP literature. Recent work on distilling BERT for classification and regression tasks shows strong performance using direct knowledge distillation. Alternatively, machine translation practitioners distill using pseudo-labeling, where a small model is trained on the translations of a larger model. A third, simpler approach is to 'shrink and fine-tune' (SFT), which avoids any explicit distillation by copying parameters to a smaller student model and then fine-tuning. We compare these three approaches for distillation of Pegasus and BART, the current and former state of the art, pre-trained summarization models, and find that SFT outperforms knowledge distillation and pseudo-labeling on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, but under-performs pseudo-labeling on the more abstractive XSUM dataset. PyTorch Code and checkpoints of different sizes are available through Hugging Face transformers here http://tiny.cc/4iy0tz.

papers_seen.title: The Role of Knowledge Distillation in Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP: Effective Practices and Limitations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, more deployable students. KD improves inference efficiency while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, but its success depends on choices of what knowledge is transferred, how the teacher and student are coupled, the match between student capacity and task complexity, and whether distillation is combined with other compression methods. Practitioners should select distillation strategies that target internal representations, task-relevant signals, and robustness properties, and consider alternative or complementary methods (e.g., structured pruning or progressive module replacement) when data, latency, or robustness constraints dictate different trade-offs.

However, the best distillation recipe depends strongly on the task, the capacity gap between teacher and student, and constraints such as data availability and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, efficient models by transferring information from one or more teacher models to a student model. The literature shows a wide variety of objectives and mechanisms for KD — from soft-target matching and internal representation alignment to adversarial, contrastive, and curriculum-inspired routes — and covers applications across vision, ranking, summarization, machine translation, and reinforcement learning. Trade-offs reported across studies include teacher–student capacity gap effects, data requirements, computational cost, robustness and generalization properties, and task-specific adaptations. Practical recipes include multi-teacher weighting, layer-wise and task-aware filters, progressive module replacement, and combinations of pruning with distillation.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to deploy large deep models by training smaller students to capture the behavior of larger teachers or ensembles. Work across computer vision, NLP, and reinforcement learning has developed complementary approaches: soft-target distillation, intermediate representation and layer-wise matching, multi- and online-teacher strategies, confidence- and task-aware weighting, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and techniques that combine distillation with structured pruning or progressive module replacement. These methods trade off fidelity to the teacher, training cost, data requirements, robustness, and runtime efficiency; their empirical success depends on design choices such as what knowledge to transfer (logits, features, attention maps, inter-channel correlations), how teachers are selected or learned, and whether the process is offline, online, or self-distillation. The literature shows that (1) distillation often reduces the effective complexity of training data and eases learning for constrained student architectures, (2) internal-representation losses, layer-wise/task-aware filtering, and route or curriculum strategies can substantially improve transfer, and (3) distillation can be combined with pruning or adversarial objectives to yield compact, fast, and sometimes robust models. Practical application requires matching the distillation recipe to task characteristics, data availability, and the student capacity.
